title: 2 Samuel 1:1–16
context: After Saul’s death, David is back in Ziklag from the campaign against the Amalekites, two days in the town, when a man arrives from Saul’s camp, clothes torn and earth on his head. He reports the defeat and the deaths of Saul and Jonathan, and, when asked how he knows, tells his own story: he happened by chance on Mount Gilboa, found Saul still alive, and, at Saul’s request, killed him and brought the crown and the bracelet to David. David and his men tear their clothes, mourn, weep, and fast until evening. Then David questions the young man again, and on the man’s own claim that he destroyed the LORD’s anointed, David has him struck down. The Amalekite’s account in verses 6–10 stands in tension with 1 Samuel 31:3–5, where Saul, distressed by the archers, asks his armor bearer to thrust him through, is refused, and “took his sword and fell on it”, after which the armor bearer sees that Saul is dead. The two reports should not be forced into a single harmonization. The narrator here presents the Amalekite’s words as his own claim. Readers have commonly taken him to have fabricated or embellished the story in hope of David’s favor; others try to read the two accounts together in some other way. Both traditions treat David’s grief and his regard for the LORD’s anointed as shared ground, not as a triumph over a rival.

verses.text: After the death of Saul, when David had returned from the slaughter of the Amalekites, and David had stayed two days in Ziklag,
verses.arminianNotes:
The book opens “After the death of Saul,” while David has returned from the slaughter of the Amalekites and has stayed two days in Ziklag. The sentence runs on into the next verse.

Arminian readers hear a real interval. Saul is dead, David is back in his town, and he has not yet heard the news. The campaign against Amalek in the previous book and the messenger who is about to appear are set side by side without comment here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the opening as a dated scene, not as David already seizing a throne. He is in Ziklag after a fight with Amalekites, and the news of Saul has not yet arrived.

Both traditions read the verse as the setting for the report that follows, shared ground at the book’s start, without turning the Amalekite campaign into a symbol beyond what the narrator states.

verses.text: on the third day, behold, a man came out of the camp from Saul, with his clothes torn and earth on his head. When he came to David, he fell to the earth and showed respect.
verses.arminianNotes:
On the third day a man comes out of the camp from Saul, with his clothes torn and earth on his head. When he comes to David, he falls to the earth and shows respect.

Arminian readers hear the signs of grief or of a report from a disaster: torn clothes, dust, and homage. The man presents himself as a bearer of hard news; what he will claim is still unheard.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that he comes “out of the camp from Saul” to David, and that the respect he shows is the prelude to a story he wants believed. The signs on his body are as the narrator describes them; their sincerity will be tested by his words.

Both traditions take the verse as the arrival of the messenger, shared narrative ground.

verses.text: David said to him, “Where do you come from?” He said to him, “I have escaped out of the camp of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David said to him, “Where do you come from?” He said to him, “I have escaped out of the camp of Israel.” David begins with a simple question, and the man locates himself as a fugitive from Israel’s camp.

Arminian readers hear a real inquiry. David does not assume the news; he asks, and the answer is that this man has escaped, a claim that will lead to the fuller report of the next verse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the question and the answer as the start of a hearing. “the camp of Israel” is the source he names; David will press for what happened there.

Both traditions read the verse as the opening exchange, shared ground, without yet judging the man’s later story.

verses.text: David said to him, “How did it go? Please tell me.” He answered, “The people have fled from the battle, and many of the people also have fallen and are dead. Saul and Jonathan his son are dead also.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David said to him, “How did it go? Please tell me.” He answered, “The people have fled from the battle, and many of the people also have fallen and are dead. Saul and Jonathan his son are dead also.”

Arminian readers hear the blow of the news itself, before the man’s personal role is claimed. The army has fled, many are dead, and Saul and Jonathan are dead also. David is told of the deaths as fact, and only then will he ask how this messenger knows.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same report: flight, slaughter, and the deaths of the king and his son. The verse does not yet say how the man knows, or what he did; it is the news David has been waiting two days without hearing.

Both traditions take the verse as the announcement of defeat and of those two deaths, shared ground of grief about to come.

verses.text: David said to the young man who told him, “How do you know that Saul and Jonathan his son are dead?”
verses.arminianNotes:
David said to the young man who told him, “How do you know that Saul and Jonathan his son are dead?” He does not yet act; he asks for the ground of the claim.

Arminian readers hear a careful question. David wants to know how this young man knows, not only what he has announced. The next verses will be the man’s own answer, and they should be heard as his claim.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the question as a pause before judgment or lament. The knowledge, not only the news, is now at issue; verses 6–10 will give the story from the messenger’s mouth.

Both traditions read the verse as David’s demand for an account, shared ground that prepares the tension with 1 Samuel 31.

verses.text: The young man who told him said, “As I happened by chance on Mount Gilboa, behold, Saul was leaning on his spear; and behold, the chariots and the horsemen followed close behind him.
verses.arminianNotes:
The young man who told him said, “As I happened by chance on Mount Gilboa, behold, Saul was leaning on his spear; and behold, the chariots and the horsemen followed close behind him.” The speech that follows, through verse 10, is introduced as what the young man said.

Arminian readers hear a story offered as chance and as eyewitness. It does not match the account in 1 Samuel 31:3–5, where Saul, distressed by the archers, is refused by his armor bearer and “took his sword and fell on it.” The tension should be named, not erased. The narrator here presents these words as the man’s own claim.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise refuse to force a single harmonization. One widely held reading is that the Amalekite fabricated or embellished the scene to win David’s favor, bringing crown and bracelet as proof. Others try to read the two accounts together in some other way. The notes cannot settle that question, and they should not invent a third narrative as if the text had supplied it.

Both traditions take verse 6 as the start of his testimony, and they keep 1 Samuel 31 in view without declaring one solution.

verses.text: When he looked behind him, he saw me and called to me. I answered, ‘Here I am.’
verses.arminianNotes:
In the same claimed scene, Saul looks behind him, sees the man, and calls; the man answers, “Here I am.” The details continue to come from the messenger’s mouth.

Arminian readers hear the story thickening as a conversation with Saul still alive. That living Saul, able to look and to call, is part of what sits uneasily beside the earlier account of his falling on his own sword. The claim remains the Amalekite’s.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that this is still the young man’s speech, not a new narrator’s confirmation. Saul, in this version, sees him and summons him; the identity question of the next verse is set up by that call.

Both traditions keep the same caution already named in verse 6: this is his account, in tension with 1 Samuel 31, and not a point of contrast between the two traditions.

verses.text: He said to me, ‘Who are you?’ I answered him, ‘I am an Amalekite.’
verses.arminianNotes:
He said to me, “Who are you?” I answered him, “I am an Amalekite.” The man reports that he named himself to Saul as an Amalekite.

Arminian readers hear the irony without pressing it into a parable: David has just returned from fighting Amalekites, and the bearer of this news says he is one. In the story he tells, Saul hears that identity before asking to be killed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the self-identification as part of the claimed dialogue. It will be confirmed again in verse 13, when David asks where he is from. The man’s people is not in doubt; the truth of his killing-story still is.

Both traditions read the verse as his own naming of himself, shared narrative ground inside the speech that began in verse 6.

verses.text: He said to me, ‘Please stand beside me, and kill me, for anguish has taken hold of me because my life lingers in me.’
verses.arminianNotes:
He reports Saul’s plea: “Please stand beside me, and kill me, for anguish has taken hold of me because my life lingers in me.” In this version Saul is in anguish, and his life has not yet gone.

Arminian readers hear a request for a finishing blow, which is not what 1 Samuel 31 records. There Saul asks his armor bearer to thrust him through, is refused, and falls on his own sword. Here the Amalekite says Saul asked him to kill him because life still lingered. The difference belongs to the tension already named; it is not to be flattened.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same claimed lingering of life, on which the next verse’s killing depends. Whether one reads the man as inventing a service he thought David would reward, or tries to read the accounts together in some other way, the notes must not declare a winner.

Both traditions take the plea as part of his testimony, and they keep David’s later judgment tied to that testimony rather than to a reconstructed harmony.

verses.text: So I stood beside him and killed him, because I was sure that he could not live after he had fallen. I took the crown that was on his head and the bracelet that was on his arm, and have brought them here to my lord.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“So I stood beside him and killed him, because I was sure that he could not live after he had fallen.” He took the crown and the bracelet and has brought them to David, “my lord.”

Arminian readers hear a confession of having killed Saul, offered with royal tokens and a hope of favor. David is addressed as lord, and the crown is in the man’s hand. The act he boasts of is exactly what verse 16 will hold against him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear the claim and the gifts together. He says he killed the king and has brought the crown and the bracelet as proof. The narrator still frames all of this as what the young man said; David’s grief will come first, and then a judgment on this mouth’s own words.

Both traditions end the speech without forcing a harmonization with 1 Samuel 31, and they treat the confession itself as the ground David will use.

verses.text: Then David took hold of his clothes and tore them; and all the men who were with him did likewise.
verses.arminianNotes:
Then David took hold of his clothes and tore them; and all the men who were with him did likewise. The first response is mourning, not reward.

Arminian readers hear a genuine grief. David does not celebrate the opening of a way to the throne; he tears his clothes, and his men do the same. The news of Saul and Jonathan is received as disaster.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same public tearing of clothes. The man who brought the crown is not thanked; the camp enters the signs of lament that verse 12 will complete.

Both traditions take the verse as shared ground in David’s regard for Saul and Jonathan, already visible before he says a word about the LORD’s anointed.

verses.text: They mourned, wept, and fasted until evening for Saul and for Jonathan his son, and for the people of the LORD, and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword.
verses.arminianNotes:
They mourned, wept, and fasted until evening for Saul and for Jonathan his son, and for the people of the LORD, and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword.

Arminian readers hear how wide the grief is: the king, the king’s son, the people of the LORD, and the house of Israel. The fast lasts until evening. This is not a private slight, and not a political show only; it is mourning for the fallen.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the fourfold object of the lament and the fast until evening as the camp’s true first work. The people of the LORD have fallen by the sword; David’s men stand with that loss.

Both traditions read the verse as shared grief for Saul, Jonathan, and Israel, the soil of the formal lament that will begin in verse 17.

verses.text: David said to the young man who told him, “Where are you from?” He answered, “I am the son of a foreigner, an Amalekite.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David said to the young man who told him, “Where are you from?” He answered, “I am the son of a foreigner, an Amalekite.” After the mourning, David returns to the messenger’s identity.

Arminian readers hear a second, calmer question. The man confirms what he already claimed on the mountain: he is an Amalekite, the son of a foreigner. He does not take refuge in being an Israelite under Israel’s law; he stands by his people and, in the next verses, by his story.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that David asks again, after the fast, and that the answer is unambiguous. The execution that follows will rest on the man’s own words about the LORD’s anointed, not on a hidden inquiry into 1 Samuel 31.

Both traditions take the verse as the confirming of his identity, shared ground before the charge of verse 14.

verses.text: David said to him, “Why were you not afraid to stretch out your hand to destroy the LORD’s anointed?”
verses.arminianNotes:
David said to him, “Why were you not afraid to stretch out your hand to destroy the LORD’s anointed?” The issue David names is fear of violating the LORD’s anointed, not the political gain of Saul’s death.

Arminian readers hear a moral and theological question. On the man’s own account he has stretched out his hand against the one the LORD had anointed. David treats that as something that should have made him afraid, even if Saul had been his enemy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the title “the LORD’s anointed.” Saul’s office is the LORD’s doing, and David will not license a killing on the plea of mercy or of opportunity. The question assumes the man’s story long enough to judge it.

Both traditions take David’s regard for the LORD’s anointed as shared ground, the heart of this unit and not a contrast between them.

verses.text: David called one of the young men and said, “Go near, and cut him down!” He struck him so that he died.
verses.arminianNotes:
David called one of the young men and said, “Go near, and cut him down!” He struck him so that he died. The judgment is immediate and is carried out by another, at David’s word.

Arminian readers hear a real sentence. David does not keep the man as a trophy of good news; he has him struck down. Whether one finds the severity hard, the text presents it as David’s act on the claim just heard, not as a later verdict of the narrator about 1 Samuel 31.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the command and the death as the outworking of verse 14. The man who said he had destroyed the LORD’s anointed is not rewarded. The next verse will state the ground: his mouth has testified against him.

Both traditions read the execution as David’s judgment on that confession, without turning it into a party debate over civil penalties.

verses.text: David said to him, “Your blood be on your head, for your mouth has testified against you, saying, ‘I have slain the LORD’s anointed.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
David said to him, “Your blood be on your head, for your mouth has testified against you, saying, ‘I have slain the LORD’s anointed.’” The man is judged by his own mouth.

Arminian readers hear why the blood is said to be on his head. David does not claim a private revelation of what happened on Gilboa; he holds the Amalekite to the words he himself has spoken. That is one reason the tension with 1 Samuel 31 can be left standing: this scene is a judgment on a claim, not a second official history of Saul’s last moment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same legal and theological line: “your mouth has testified against you,” and the confessed slaying of the LORD’s anointed is enough for this sentence. Readers who think the story was invented and readers who try to read the accounts together can still agree that David refuses to profit from, or to honor, a hand stretched out against the LORD’s anointed.

Both traditions close the unit on that shared ground, without declaring how the two reports of Saul’s death are finally to be combined.
